intro: What a standard variable rate is, when a mortgage moves onto it, how the lender sets it, and how it differs from fixed and tracker deals.
explanation:
## An SVR is a lender's own variable rate, and it is what many deals end on

A standard variable rate (SVR) is a variable rate that the lender sets for itself. The reason most borrowers meet one is the reversion rate, which is the rate a mortgage moves onto when its initial fixed or discounted period ends. A borrower who arranges nothing is moved onto the lender's reversion rate automatically. In many cases that rate is an SVR, though lenders can use a different kind of rate, and it normally costs more than the deal that has ended.

The Bank of England publishes an average of the standard variable rates that UK lenders charge, which it calls revert-to rates. It is a market average, and each lender sets its own.

## The lender sets the rate, and it is not tied to Bank Rate

An SVR is not linked directly to an outside rate. The lender decides it, and can change it whenever its terms allow. That separates it from a tracker mortgage, which follows the Bank of England's Bank Rate, covered on the [Bank of England Base Rate](/uk/mortgages/interest-rates/bank-of-england-base-rate/) page. Bank Rate still matters to lenders, as it affects borrowing costs across the economy, but for loans the Bank says other things count as well, including the lender's view of the risk of the loan and how long the loan is for.

Because the rate can change, the monthly payment on an SVR is not fixed in the way it is on a fixed-rate deal.

## Moving off an SVR means arranging a replacement deal

A mortgage offer is generally valid for 3 to 6 months, depending on the lender, so a replacement deal can be arranged before the current one ends and set to start the day it finishes. A borrower who is up to date with payments and stays with the same lender should be able to switch without an affordability check, unless they want to borrow more. Moving to a different lender normally brings an affordability check.

Leaving a fixed or discounted deal early can mean an early repayment charge, usually a percentage of the remaining balance, so whether one applies depends on the terms of the mortgage.
